newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian unions to continue phone, postal strike.
newsitem.headline: Indian unions to continue phone, postal strike.

text.p: Indian trade unions on Friday vowed to continue a nationwide strike that has thrown phone and postal services into disarray, dashing hopes for a quick end to the three-day work stoppage by more than one million employees.
"The strike will continue," R.K. Kohli, assistant general secretary of the National Federation of Telecom Employees, told Reuters following a meeting of six unions leading the stoppage.

The unions rejected a government promise to consider their demand for the elimination of a ceiling on annual pay bonuses, arguing that a cap on bonuses for railway workers had already been lifted and set a precedent.
"The decision has been taken to continue the strike until a cabinet decision," Kohli said.

Army experts have been supporting telecommunications and postal services for the past two days, an army spokesman told Reuters. Army officers were providing security at post offices and helping deliver important mail, he said.
The spokesman could not say how may army personnel were involved.
Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda was travelling in northeastern India and not expected back in Delhi until next week. A cabinet meeting was tentatively set for next Tuesday.
Earlier on Friday, the federation's general secretary, O.P. Gupta, and a senior government official said they expected the strike to be called off soon, perhaps later in the day.

But Kohli said the six unions -- three representing telecommunications workers, three others in the postal sector -- agreed that verbal assurances that their complaint would be taken up by Deve Gowda's cabinet were inadequate.

A government official who asked not to be identified said negotiations had snagged on union demands that striking employees be paid for days missed during the strike, while the government wanted them to forgo leave in exchange.
At the outset of the strike, some government officials had said fiscal austerity demanded the 3,500-rupee ($100) ceiling on bonuses for telecommunications and postal workers be retained.
The government, concerned over high interest rates and the cost of debt, has set itself an ambitious austerity target.
On the first day of the strike, Communications Minister Beni Prasad Varma called the work stoppage illegal, saying the unions had not given adequate advance notice.
But both Varma and Finance Minister P. Chidambaram quickly sought to assuage the striking workers, saying their demands deserved a sympathetic hearing.
The strike has crippled postal services with millions of letters piling up in post offices across the nation. Private courier services said they reaped a windfall.
Telecommunications services, which are largely automated, have fared better than the post. But operator-related services and repair and maintenance were badly disrupted.

V.L. Narayan, telecommunications expert at the Federation of Indian Chambers of Commerce and Industry (FICCI), said there were no reliable estimates of the value of business that may have been lost due to the strike.
He said companies in India were accustomed to breakdowns in power and phone services, and many had begun resorting to private courier companies to deliver mail.
